activities.caption: pair each decision family with its question
activities.name: didThreeMatch

config.prompt: Three decisions dominate every interface — pair each with the question it answers:

pairs.right: what matters most — what the user sees first
what looks usable before anyone touches it
making wrong actions impossible or unlikely

config.why: Design is deciding on the user's behalf — hundreds of small decisions made so coherently the product is obvious before you think.

activities.anchor: the beautiful interface that assumes silence, two free hands and perfect connectivity
activities.caption: file each pressure under its context dimension
activities.name: didContextSort

config.prompt: A job under conditions — file each pressure:

items.label: a pedestrian in Tokyo rain versus a courier on a bike
an interface used hourly must be fast and muscle-memorised
one used yearly must be self-explanatory
a music app's undo versus a medical pump's dosing error
standards of certainty set by what failure costs

config.why: The same map app is a different product for three users — every design decision made without its context is the classic failure mode.

activities.anchor: the office chair, the car seat, the standing desk
activities.caption: call Daniels's 1950 sample
activities.name: didDanielsEst

config.prompt: The measurement that grounded the modern adjustable cockpit — roughly how many pilots did Gilbert Daniels measure against five body dimensions in 1950?
config.why: Over 4,000 — and a cockpit built for the average on all five would fit approximately nobody.
config.context: Clearance dimensions for the large percentile, reach dimensions for the small, adjustability in between.

activities.anchor: the feedback loop between user and tool
activities.caption: find the faulty line — design for safety
activities.name: didSafetySpot

config.prompt: One of these safety-design claims is backwards — click it:
lines: Ergonomics generalises fit from size to load: cognitive load, posture over time, force required.
After Three Mile Island (1979), regulators required better control-room instrumentation and training.
Guard the hazard, fail visibly rather than silently, use interlocks where error is costly.
The WHO surgical safety checklist is a procedure document, not a designed object.
Designing for the edge case improves the product for everyone.
config.correction: It is a designed object, as much as any chair — checklists are interaction design with lives in the balance.
config.why: Interface decisions become public safety — which is why safety design has reusable moves instead of hopes.

activities.anchor: the Gestalt law of proximity doing layout work
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the psychology of obvious
activities.name: didNormanCloze

config.text: Controls should correspond spatially to their effects — stove knobs laid out like the %%0%% they fire. Make wrong actions impossible: the %%1%% plug that cannot be inserted wrong. And in hierarchy, %%2%% is the lever — size, weight, colour and whitespace all shout.
config.hint: The kitchen, the plug, and the lever that decides what a user sees first.

activities.anchor: design's shadow side, where the same skill that extends a product's useful life is used to curtail it
activities.caption: which R is this decision?
activities.name: didSixRSort

config.prompt: The sustainability hierarchy in action — file each decision:
buckets: Reduce / Reuse — material and second life

items.label: a library of tools instead of everyone owning a drill
no plastic film on a cucumber, no bundled charger
modular phones built for a second life
screws instead of glue, standard parts, published manuals

config.why: The hierarchy exists because designers instinctively reach for the last R when the first one was the real answer.

activities.anchor: as the behavioural-economics literature on organ-donation consent rates shows
activities.caption: walk the dark-pattern decision
activities.name: didDarkBranch

config.root: The growth team proposes hiding the cancel link three menus deep and pre-ticking the marketing-consent box. Walk the call.

choices.label: Dark patterns — confirm-shaming, hidden costs, roach motels
choices.feedback: The term is Brignull's, 2010 — and the expertise that places a primary action under the thumb can place the cancel link where the thumb never goes.

choices.label: Persuasive design — nothing to see here
choices.feedback: The same lever, aimed: which is exactly why aiming it at users is the ethical line, not a grey zone.

choices.label: Ship it — the engagement metrics will thank us
choices.feedback: Weaponised defaults trade short-term numbers for the trust the product runs on.

choices.label: Refuse — honest defaults, an equally reachable cancel
choices.feedback: Ethics is not adjacent to this subject; it is the same lever, aimed well.

persuade.text: Defaults are decisions — the most powerful ones a designer makes — and that power is what makes the ethics non-optional.

shipped.text: Easy to enter, designed to be hard to leave: the roach motel ships, and the apology comes later.

refused.text: The designed honest path costs growth now and compounds trust — the decision a strategy can defend.

config.why: Design creates markets and shapes behaviour — defaults, chimes, dark patterns — and every one of those is a decision someone made deliberately.

activities.anchor: a message that quietly fails after appearing to send is worse than a visible spinner
activities.caption: place the perception threshold
activities.name: didThresholdPlace

config.prompt: Every user action needs a visible result within roughly how many milliseconds?
config.why: About 100 ms — the perception threshold; past about a second a felt pause, past ten seconds the abandonment risk that sets the loading-state budget.
